subject: Maths
central_question: How can data be collected, represented and analysed with mean, median, variability and graphs to make justified conclusions without overgeneralising?
in_scope_units: 5.1 Of Questions and Statements: distinguishing statistical questions and statements and recognising the need to collect variable data.
5.2 Representative Values: comparing data groups using totals, arithmetic mean and the fair-share interpretation.
Know Your Onions and Dot Plots: comparing minimum, maximum, range, total, mean, clusters and spread while noting that order information may be lost.
Averages Around Us, Outliers and Medians: finding medians for odd and even data sets and studying how outliers affect the mean.
Measures of Central Tendency and Variability: using mean, median, minimum and maximum together to describe data.
Zero versus No Value and A Mean Foot: distinguishing a recorded zero from an absent observation and viewing the mean as equalisation.
5.3 Visualising Data: reading and constructing clustered or double-column graphs and following the two-step identify-and-infer process.
Rocket launches, daylight hours and cricket graphs: interpreting scale, trends, categories and claims supported by a graph.
5.4 Data Detective: examining height data over grades, ages, years and countries and avoiding unsupported generalisations.
Final Figure it Out and Projects: solving Questions 1–13 and conducting individual or group data investigations.
banned_topics: Mode as a required measure, because the chapter focuses on mean and median.
Formal standard deviation, variance and quartiles.
Pie charts and histograms as construction topics.
Causal claims that cannot be established from the displayed data.

known_pitfalls.claim: A total is always enough to compare two groups.
known_pitfalls.correction: If group sizes differ, compare a representative value such as the mean rather than totals alone.

known_pitfalls.claim: The median is the middle entry in the order originally given.
known_pitfalls.correction: The data must first be sorted; with an even number of values, average the two middle values.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mean always represents typical data well.
known_pitfalls.correction: A very high or low outlier can pull the mean away from most values, while the median is usually less affected.

known_pitfalls.claim: A score of zero and an absent observation are the same.
known_pitfalls.correction: Zero is a recorded value and is included, while a dash meaning did not play or was absent is not counted as a data value.

known_pitfalls.claim: A graph proves any general claim about all people or all future years.
known_pitfalls.correction: Conclusions must stay within the population, categories and time period represented by the data.

known_pitfalls.claim: A dot plot preserves the original month-by-month order.
known_pitfalls.correction: A dot plot displays frequency, clustering and spread but may lose the original sequence of observations.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with Section 5.1's list of questions to classify statistical and non-statistical questions.
Use the guava fair-share activity and the Hibiscus data on page 100 to build the arithmetic mean.
Use Figure it Out Question 1 on page 101 to calculate the mean of Shreyas's eight bounce counts.
Use the Yahapur and Wahapur onion tables and dot plots on pages 101–103 to compare centre and spread.
Use the two family-height examples on pages 105–108 to introduce median and outliers.
Use the rocket-launch and daylight graphs on pages 115–120 to practise the identify-and-infer process.
Conclude with Data Detective and final Figure it Out Questions 1–13 on pages 129–134.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The concluding Figure it Out section on pages 129–134 contains Questions 1–13, including projects, followed by the chapter summary.
